newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts top European high-yielder charts.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts top European high-yielder charts.

text.p: UK gilts confirmed their status as the new high yielders of Europe on Thursday as the 10-year spread over Bunds widened to 202 basis points following a jump in core UK inflation in October to 3.3 percent.
With interest rate concerns and political risk seen dogging the beleagured market for some months yet, analysts said these levels would likely persist in the near term.
"Gilts stand out like a sore thumb at the moment," said Brian Hilliard, chief economist of the fixed income division at Societe Generale.

"These spreads are certainly justified in the short term. But I'm encourged by the renewed buying interest whenever we hit 200. There seems to be some realisation that even in the short term, if it goes above that...gilts are looking very cheap."

One dealer said there was some switching out of Bunds into gilts when the spread hit 202. Volumes in the gilt future in morning trade was higher than that in the Bund, a very rare occurrence, he added.
Hilliard expected the 10-year gilt/Bund spread to widen out to 210 to 220 basis points in the near term.
Steve Scott, gilts analyst at Kleinwort Benson, said the ailing market was suffering from a lack of confidence.
"These spreads show the market has now got long term value but is suffering short term confidence problems," he said.
The flurry of EMU convergence trades in the last six months have given traditional high yielding debt such as Italian BTPs a welcome leg up and left gilts out in the cold.
The Italian government is trying to slash its debt in line with EMU convergence criteria, a move the market appears to see as sufficient to ensure its entry to a single European currency.

By 1418 GMT, the 10-year gilt spread over Bunds was off its earlier 200 level at 197 basis points, 20 basis points higher than Italian BTPs. Even peripheral European bonds such as Finnish debt offer investors a lower yield.

Analysts said EMU convergence trades were only part of the picture. Uncertainty about the forthcoming general election, inflation worries and the fact the British economic cycle is out of sync with the rest of Europe, are all weighing heavily on the curve.
The ruling Conservative party, which continues to lag Labour in the polls, must hold a general election by May 22.
Hilliard said uncertainty about the policies of a Labour government was a key stumbling block for the market.

"There is a possibility that Labour will have such a lead and such clear policies that the uncertainty will be dispelled before the election. Once that happens, and the market is convinced that Labour party policies are as prudent as they say they are....you'll see a return to the 160 level," he said.
Thursday's brush with a 202 basis point spread was sparked by renewed inflation concerns as headline inflation jumped to 2.7 percent in October from 2.1 percent in September.
The core rate, excluding mortgage interest payments, crept further away from the government's 2.5 percent inflation target, rising to 3.3 percent from September's 2.9 percent.
Coming on top of alarmingly strong labour market data on Wednesday, the figures increase the likelihood of a further pre-election rate rise, analysts said.
"There's a reluctance to buy until the situation becomes clearer," said one trader. "Once the budget is past us you might see that spread coming in a little bit."
The November 26 budget is widely expected to contain up to three billion sterling of tax cuts.
"But I'd be surprised if we get much below 195 in the near term," the dealer said. "We won't get to the 170s or 180s for a long time yet."
